title: A disabled theatre troupe makes the able-bodied the discriminated minority — and it isn't asking for your sympathy
dek: Yaoyao flips the whole social order: after a nuclear war most people are augmented, and the unaugmented able-bodied few become the Sinners, the ones who have to fight for their rights. This isn't a lament — it's a power fantasy written for disabled people.
why: Mostly oral testimony, with no data or research framework; the value is in the concrete scenes and in how a single play grew. Anyone looking for methodology or industry judgment can skip it.
who: People working in public welfare, theatre and community workshops; content people trying to understand why integration can't rest on goodwill alone; practitioners and volunteers in disability issues.
skip: The rehearsal clip at the start and the submission call-out at the end can be skipped.

points.h: Disabled women being unable to leave the house is the norm
points.body: Yaoyao's earliest work was the documentary Han Ya (寒鸦), about three disabled women's struggles with family education and employment. One of the sisters had not left her home in 36 years; when her parents took her out to visit relatives at New Year, her feeling was ‘like walking a little dog or cat’. Later she got the first computer of her life, went online, and found a job as a telephone operator — no degree required, only a sweet voice. Once she had the job she bought herself a wheelchair and rolled out of the house. Another mother, visually impaired, was allowed to breastfeed her newborn for only five minutes before her mother-in-law took the baby away, on the grounds that ‘you can't see, you can't raise a child’; for years afterward she fought her husband's family for custody. These accounts made Yaoyao realise that being unable to leave the house was not an isolated case.

points.h: Every friend a disabled person has is also disabled
points.body: A former colleague of Yaoyao's uses a wheelchair, and when she moved she could only ask friends who also use wheelchairs; they hung the chairs front and back with belongings and hauled load after load. Yaoyao instinctively asked why she didn't call able-bodied friends who can walk upright to help — it would be done in half a day. The colleague paused, then said, I don't know any able-bodied people — she did not have a single able-bodied friend, and even her friends all used wheelchairs. Yaoyao says she didn't know how to continue the conversation, and realised only one thing: if disabled and able-bodied people never even get the chance to meet, ‘you have no chance at integration to speak of’. That was the direct starting point for her later search for a drama teacher and for making integrated theatre.

points.h: The able-bodied are written as the discriminated Sinners
points.body: Leyi Theatre's first play, Reverse Future (逆转未来), does a straight identity reversal: a nuclear war turns most people disabled, and they become new humans through technological modification — electronic eyes, cochlear implants and the like; the surviving able-bodied minority, guilty of ‘the crime of starting the nuclear war’, become the Sinners, marginalised by society. Yaoyao's logic is that since she herself is a situs inversus person, she might as well flip the whole society too, turning every right disabled people now have to fight for into a right the able-bodied have to fight for — what she calls writing a power fantasy for disabled people. The core of the plot: a Sinner father, to spare his son from suffering for his able body, gets drunk, picks up a chainsaw and tries to saw off his son's legs, but ends up in a pool of blood himself; the son is charged with patricide, and the courtroom scenes open up the debate about Sinners and augmented humans.

points.h: How the unseen and the unheard partner up
points.body: Visually impaired actor Wang Xiaomin was pulled in as a partner by deaf actor Li Ning during an audition, and his first reaction was blank: you can't hear, I can't see, how are we supposed to act. Li Ning's solution was to put his hand on the back of Wang's hand and trace, tapping once when it was Wang's line. Director Ma Yan says blind and deaf performers sharing a stage already exists abroad: the deaf person's hand rests on the visually impaired person's hand, and the visually impaired person can feel the movements. Wang Xiaomin says deaf people had been around him since childhood, but back then he saw them as two kinds of people born with a communication barrier, ‘absolutely no way they could ever communicate’, a barrier that was almost insurmountable — after this collaboration he and Li Ning became very good friends. The troupe also had to solve sign language interpretation, real-time captioning on a big screen, and a volunteer doing audio description for each visually impaired actor.

points.h: Visually impaired actors cheat on stage with earphones
points.body: Only later in rehearsals did the director discover that the visually impaired actors were in fact ‘cheating’: they wore earphones, listened to their lines at several times normal speed, and delivered them live on stage without any trouble, so the director had no way to assess them and could only marvel at how fast the visually impaired actors got their lines down. Conversely, the director doesn't know sign language, so he could only watch everyone signing while he laughed along, when in fact the actors might be complaining about him in sign. Once they got to know each other, everyone's little tricks came out.

points.h: She got the best production award from the ICU
points.body: In 2024 Reverse Future was selected for the Nanjing New Theatre Festival initiated by Stan Lai. That year Yaoyao had heart problems and went into the ICU; the troupe nearly fell apart, and it was a friend who stepped in to gather everyone for rehearsals and take them to Nanjing. At the closing buffet, while the other groups' tables sat empty and their members dressed up waiting for the awards, only their table kept going back for more food, thinking ‘how could it possibly be us’. In the end they won Best Production, the festival's highest award, and jury chairman Stan Lai stood up and led the applause. The news reached the ICU at the same moment as the award, and Yaoyao lay in her hospital bed in tears. That October the play was invited to the Wuzhen Theatre Festival, the first integrated disability production, and the only piece in the ‘Nothing Is Impossible’ section.

points.h: After writing this play she changed her answer on being born
points.body: The second play, I Choose to Be Born (我选择出生), is set in a world where every country legislates that when a fetus reaches eight months, parents must use brainwaves to inform it of its health and family circumstances, and the fetus decides whether to be born. Among five families: deaf parents who must truthfully tell their child you will be deaf too; a husband who deceives his wife into having a child; a family that favours boys over girls; and a final story adapted from Yaoyao's own experience. The troupe's actors couldn't get through the script, because their life experiences were eerily similar — only the conditions differed. Asked whether they would still choose to be born given another chance, most of the troupe still said they would choose birth, because they still love this world; Yaoyao changed her answer: she used to say she would choose birth too, but now she might choose not to be born, because disabled people are forced to be born into this society, with no choice at all.

points.h: Cai Cong and she give opposite answers to the same question
points.body: The episode sets the deaf couple in I Choose to Be Born against the real Cai Cong (蔡聪): Cai Cong and his wife are both visually impaired, and when his wife was pregnant many people urged them to get tests to see whether the child would inherit the visual impairment, but Cai Cong did not want the mere possibility that the child might also be visually impaired to predetermine that such a life was not worth starting; they believe they can give a child a loving family. The deaf couple in the play decide to let the child be born. Yaoyao and Cai Cong give very different answers, and the argument around this choice persists. The question the episode poses: when a family makes a choice, how much capacity to choose does it actually have.

quotes.text: She was taken aback too, and said, I don't know any able-bodied people. She didn't have a single able-bodied friend — even she and her friends all used wheelchairs.
I said, I'm a situs inversus person, so we might as well flip the whole society too and see what happens.
This play makes you think. The sincerity of the performance covers the flaws in technique. What is most striking is the troupe's refusal to be pitied.
None of us could get through it, because we felt our life experiences were so eerily similar — only the conditions were different, but the experiences were the same.
